items.followUp: Why are gases more compressible than liquids?

rubric.why: Identifies the large spaces between gas particles.
rubric.description: States that gas particles are far apart, with large intermolecular spaces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the large spaces between gas particles as the reason for their low density compared with liquids.

rubric.why: Links the particle spacing to lower density.
rubric.description: Explains that gases have less mass per unit volume than liquids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the low number of particles, or low mass, in a given volume results in lower density.

modelAnswer: Gas particles are much farther apart than particles in liquids, so there are fewer particles in a given volume.
Therefore, gases have less mass per unit volume and lower density than liquids.

items.followUp: What does m/v % mean for a solution?

rubric.why: Gives the defining quantities for volume/mass percentage.
rubric.description: Defines V/m % as the volume of solute present in 100 g of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the volume of solute and the 100 g of solution basis.

rubric.description: Gives the volume/mass percentage formula or its equivalent interpretation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the relationship: volume of solute divided by mass of solution, multiplied by 100.

modelAnswer: V/m % is the volume of solute, in cm³, present in 100 g of solution.
V/m % = (volume of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100.

items.followUp: What happens to the concentration of a solution when more solvent is added?

rubric.why: Identifies how dilution is carried out.
rubric.description: States that dilution is carried out by adding more solvent to a solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the addition of solvent as the process.

rubric.description: States that adding solvent decreases the solution's concentration while the amount of solute remains unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the decrease in concentration or the unchanged amount of solute.

modelAnswer: Dilution is carried out by adding more solvent to a solution.
The amount of solute remains unchanged, but the concentration of the solution decreases.

items.followUp: Why does a solution, unlike a suspension, have a uniform composition?

rubric.why: Identifies the nature of suspension particles.
rubric.description: States that suspension particles remain undissolved or are relatively large.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the undissolved or large particles in a suspension.

rubric.why: Explains why the mixture is not homogeneous.
rubric.description: Explains that suspension particles are unevenly distributed or settle on standing, so the composition is not uniform.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking uneven distribution or settling to the lack of homogeneity.

modelAnswer: The particles of a suspension do not dissolve and are relatively large.
They are not uniformly distributed and may settle on standing, so the suspension is not homogeneous.

items.followUp: What happens when aluminium is exposed to air?

rubric.why: Distinguishes aluminium from iron, which forms rust.
rubric.description: States that aluminium does not rust.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating that aluminium does not form rust.

rubric.why: Recognizes the protective surface layer aluminium forms.
rubric.description: States that aluminium forms a protective oxide layer on its surface.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the oxide layer and its protective nature.

modelAnswer: No. Aluminium does not rust; rust is iron oxide.
Aluminium forms a thin, protective layer of aluminium oxide on its surface.

rubric.why: Credits one correct example of a very reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example, such as sodium, potassium or lithium.

rubric.description: Names a second very reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second correct example; do not award the mark for repeating the first example.

modelAnswer: Sodium and potassium are two very reactive metals.

items.followUp: Name two non-metals that are important components of living organisms.

rubric.why: Identifies the role of oxygen in sustaining life.
rubric.description: States that oxygen is needed for respiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking oxygen with respiration.

rubric.why: Identifies another life-essential role of non-metals.
rubric.description: States that carbon is a basic component of organic compounds, or that nitrogen is needed to form proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct role of carbon or nitrogen in living organisms.

modelAnswer: Oxygen is essential for respiration in living organisms.
Carbon forms the basic framework of organic compounds, and nitrogen is needed to make proteins.

items.followUp: How does metallic character change across a period and down a group?

rubric.why: States the trend across a period.
rubric.description: Non-metallic character increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct left-to-right trend across a period.

rubric.why: States the trend down a group.
rubric.description: Non-metallic character decreases down a group (or increases up a group).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct trend within a group.

modelAnswer: Across a period, non-metallic character increases from left to right.
Down a group, non-metallic character decreases (it increases from bottom to top).
